Linearised inference for weighted LMTP policy means and additive contrasts

Source: R/margot_lmtp_linearised_inference.R
margot_lmtp_linearised_inference.Rd

`margot_lmtp_linearised_inference()` recomputes the standard error of a weighted policy-specific mean, or of an additive contrast between two policy means fitted to the same participants, from the pseudo-outcomes and weights stored in `lmtp` fits. It uses the linearisation of the weighted (Hájek) mean, $$\hat\theta = \sum_i w_i \varphi_i / \sum_i w_i, \qquad \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat\theta) = \{ s^2(u) / n \}^{1/2}, \qquad u_i = w_i(\varphi_i - \hat\theta)/\bar w,$$ where \(\hat\theta\) is the estimate stored in the fit (for the SDR estimator, the weighted mean shown), \(\varphi_i\) is participant \(i\)'s uncentred pseudo-outcome, \(w_i\) the baseline weight, \(\bar w\) the mean weight and \(s^2\) the sample variance. For a contrast, \(\varphi_i\) is the difference of the two pseudo-outcomes. With repeated identifiers, the contributions are summed within clusters and the cluster-robust form used by `ife` is applied.

Usage

margot_lmtp_linearised_inference(fit, ref = NULL, conf_level = NULL)

Arguments

fit

An `lmtp` fit, or the `ife` estimate stored in its `estimate` element.

ref

Optional reference fit of the same form. When supplied, the function reports the additive contrast `fit` minus `ref`. Both fits must carry identical weights and identifiers.

conf_level

Confidence level for the two-sided Wald interval. Defaults to the level implied by the critical value stored in `fit`.

Value

A one-row data frame with the estimate, the linearised standard error, interval limits, a two-sided p-value against zero (contrasts only), the standard error reported by `lmtp`, the number of participants and clusters, and the variance method.

Details

`lmtp` 1.5.4 with `ife` 0.2.5 computes \(s^2(w_i\varphi_i)/n\), which centres the weighted product rather than the pseudo-outcome; with repeated identifiers it sums the uncentred products within clusters. The two agree when the weights are constant and no identifier repeats. They differ when the weights vary, and with clusters of unequal size even under constant weights. The difference can be large for policy means on a scale far from zero and depends on the contrast's size for additive contrasts. Point estimates are unchanged. The function fits no model and does not account for estimation of the weights.
